item.title: Generative deep-learning-embedded asynchronous structured light for three-dimensional imaging
item.description:
The problem

Structured light measures 3D shape by projecting a sequence of stripe images, called fringe patterns, onto an object and photographing them from a second viewpoint. The surface bends the stripes, and the stripe phase at each pixel encodes depth. In fringe projection profilometry (FPP), one of the most popular forms of the technique, the camera must capture each pattern while it alone is on screen. That requires synchronisation between projector and camera, usually a hardware trigger signal.

Synchronisation is a practical burden. Hardware trigger circuits are found in expensive industrial equipment, while affordable consumer devices often have no interface for them, even though the cameras in smartphones, tablets and laptops now offer high resolution and frame rates. Software synchronisation waits longer than the exposure time between patterns, which lowers the frame rate and does not always work stably. Signal wires also limit how far apart camera and projector can be and are susceptible to electromagnetic interference. If projector and camera simply run independently, though, the projector can switch patterns in the middle of an exposure, and the photo records a blend of two neighbouring patterns: an aliased fringe pattern (AFP). Computing phase directly from such images leads to reconstruction errors. Earlier work on unsynchronised structured light used simple binary (black-and-white) patterns or addressed other aspects of asynchrony; to the authors’ knowledge, asynchronous capture with the widely used sinusoidal fringes had not been studied.

How it works

The mixing itself has a simple form. Each pixel of an AFP adds up what the two patterns contributed during the exposure, and the split depends on the moment the projector switched (Eq. 5). The mixing does not move pixels; it is the same at every location, a property that suits a convolutional network. The switching moment, however, is unknown and very difficult to measure, so recovering two images from one is an ill-posed, one-to-many problem. The paper treats it as image generation: a generative network learns to produce the two clean patterns, and standard phase-shifting reconstruction then applies unchanged.

  1. Synchronised capture (the reference). Each exposure sees exactly one projected pattern, so each photo holds one clean pattern.
  2. Asynchronous capture. Projector and camera each run at their own constant speed, with the camera faster so that every pattern is captured. A pattern switch inside an exposure produces an AFP that integrates the two neighbouring patterns. The paper addresses mixes of two patterns.
  3. Separation with APSNet. APSNet (aliased fringe pattern separation network) is an encoder–decoder based on U-Net: four encoding blocks with max pooling, then a decoder that upsamples with skip connections back to full resolution. It maps one AFP to the two patterns it was mixed from. It is trained as the generator of a conditional generative adversarial network (GAN): a discriminator judges generated pattern pairs against real ones, and two further loss terms, mean-squared error and structural similarity, keep the generated patterns statistically close to the projected ones. Equal weights for the three terms gave the smoothest training (Fig. 8).
  4. Phase. From three AFPs, APSNet yields four successive patterns, each shifted by a quarter period. The well-established four-step phase-shifting algorithm computes the wrapped phase, and adding the fringe order (multiples of 2π) unwraps it into a continuous phase map.
  5. 3D shape. The continuous phase is converted into the object’s 3D shape with an established FPP reconstruction model.

The training data come from a real system: an industrial camera (2048 × 1536 pixels), a DLP projector (1280 × 1024) and a self-developed microcontroller that delays the camera by a set time Δt after the projector. With Δt = 0 the system captures ordinary, non-aliased fringes. The source patterns were five sets of 256 × 256 sinusoidal fringes with 50 to 90 periods, each in four phase shifts (0, 0.5π, π, 1.5π), captured with delays from 1 to 10 ms in 1 ms steps. This gave 1500 AFPs, each paired with its two source patterns: 1125 for training and 375 for testing.

Results

Within 0.008 mm of the synchronised reconstruction along a depth profile of a statue, with a standard deviation of 0.003 mm. Depth computed directly from the AFPs is off by −5.000 to 3.600 mm, with a standard deviation of 1.713 mm (Fig. 13).
Wrapped phase within 0.035 rad of the synchronised phase along a sampled line (Fig. 11).
Absolute error below 0.006 mm on a propeller and a 3D-printed bolt, objects with large-curvature surfaces absent from the earlier tests (standard deviations 0.002 and 0.001 mm; Fig. 16).

The test objects, including statues, a car model and a sphere, were not seen by the network during training or validation. Every comparison treats the reconstruction from synchronised patterns as the benchmark. Reconstructing directly from the AFPs loses much of the shape, while the shape from APSNet’s patterns is remarkably close to the benchmark (Fig. 12). In the paper’s summary, this improves reconstruction accuracy by three orders of magnitude over using the aliased fringes directly.

The network was trained only on sinusoidal patterns, yet it also separated aliased binary patterns projected onto a sphere, a car model and a statue, without further tuning (Fig. 14). It also handled a multi-object scene of a propeller prototype, a 3D-printed bolt and a statue, with different colours and reflective materials (Fig. 15). The method assumes that each photo mixes two patterns. If the projector runs much faster than the camera, more than two patterns fall within one exposure; the authors name this more complex aliasing as a limitation and a direction for further work.

item.title: Deep learning-enabled 3D multimodal fusion of cone-beam CT and intraoral mesh scans for clinically applicable tooth-bone reconstruction
item.description:
The problem

Orthodontic treatment and implant surgery are planned on 3D models of the teeth and the bone that holds them. Two kinds of scan feed these models, and each sees only part of the picture. Cone-beam CT (CBCT) is an X-ray scan that shows whole teeth, crowns and roots, inside the jaw bone. But CBCT measurements can be up to 6.9% smaller than the real objects, depending on resolution, and CBCT often fails to capture the biting surfaces accurately because of dense enamel, dental restorations, implants and orthodontic appliances. An intraoral scanner (IOS) projects light onto the teeth and records a digital impression as a surface mesh. Its shrinkage can be as low as 0.9%, making it the most accurate of the 3D digital modalities, and it captures the bite and tooth positions well, but it shows only the crowns and gums, nothing below the gum line.

Combining the two gives what clinicians need: precise crowns on the correct roots, inside the surrounding bone. Doing this by hand is slow. Both scans must first be segmented, which is hard because anatomy varies from patient to patient. The CBCT usually shows the upper and lower jaws together, often in a bite where teeth touch, while the IOS records each jaw separately. Experienced experts need at least five hours per patient, even with interactive software and semi-automatic tools, and a fully automatic, clinically applicable solution had yet to be developed.

How it works

Deep Dental Multimodal Fusion (DDMF) is an automatic pipeline with three modules: segment the CBCT, segment the intraoral scan, then fuse the two. The fused model takes the crowns from the IOS and the roots and bone from the CBCT.

  1. Segment the CBCT. TSTNet, a network built on the Swin Transformer, labels every pixel of each 2D CBCT slice as tooth, alveolar bone or background, and 3D meshes of the teeth and bone are reconstructed from the result. Training needs labels on only about 20 of the 300–600 slices in a scan. An extra training head, tooth error calibration (TEC), corrects error-prone pixels at the tooth–bone boundary; it is removed at inference, so it adds no inference time.
  2. Segment the intraoral scan. IOSNet labels each face of the IOS mesh as gum or as one of 32 teeth, numbered in the FDI system. Two new training losses help: a centroid loss keeps the predicted centre of each tooth in place, so that two teeth are not recognised as one (or one as two), and a boundary loss sharpens tooth–tooth and tooth–gum borders. The gum is then separated, leaving numbered crowns.
  3. Split the jaws in the CBCT. A point-curvature feature, the average angle between a vertex’s surface normal and those of its neighbours, marks the boundaries where teeth meet. Removing the highest-curvature vertices separates the individual teeth; the removed vertices are merged back, and the teeth are grouped into upper and lower jaws.
  4. Register. The IOS crowns of each jaw are aligned with the matching CBCT jaw in two stages: a global registration (RANSAC on FPFH features) gives a rough initial alignment, and point-to-plane ICP at three scales refines it.
  5. Replace the crowns and fuse. CBCT crown points that lie close to the IOS crown are removed and replaced with the IOS points, and Poisson reconstruction turns the merged points into one mesh. The FDI tooth numbers come from the IOS, so the fused teeth are identified individually without instance-level annotation of the CBCT slices.

Results

Average surface distance of 0.17 mm between the fused models and expert-made ground truth, over 1,003 teeth in 50 cases (Chamfer distance 0.20 mm, Hausdorff distance 0.37 mm; Table 3).
20–25 minutes per patient, against 300–400 minutes for human experts (Table 6).
94% of CBCT meshes split correctly into upper and lower jaws, against 42% for a Gaussian-curvature method and 24% for DBSCAN, on 50 patients, 31 of them in a closed bite with tight contacts (Table 5).

The study used a large real-world dataset: 503 patients with both CBCT and intraoral scans, plus 28,559 further intraoral scans, collected from hospitals and clinics in 25 provinces of China from 2018 to 2021. The ground-truth fused models were made by a committee of human experts and had been used successfully in clinical practice. The errors were small and consistent across tooth types; the first and second molars showed slightly larger errors, mainly because they are larger. Since CBCT resolution ranged from 0.125 to 0.5 mm, an error of one to two pixels is acceptable for many clinical applications, as validated by human experts and a clinical applicability test. On 20 cases, DDMF also had lower errors than reconstruction from CBCT alone (Fig. 4C–E). The paper reports no other fusion baseline, as no systematic solution existed for this task.

Each segmentation module outperformed the compared networks. TSTNet reached a Dice coefficient of 93.99% in 5-fold cross-validation, with 50 test patients per fold, ahead of UNet, UNet++, the standard Swin Transformer and the other baselines (Table 1). IOSNet (trained on 28,000 scans) reached a mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 93.70% on lower-jaw scans and 95.70% on upper-jaw scans, 1.77 and 3.52 points above DCNet, the strongest baseline (Table 2).

The framework has been integrated into clinical software that assists orthodontic treatment planning. The authors also name its limits. The jaw splitting and registration steps may fail in 6–10% of cases, which then need manual correction, and segmentation may still be error-prone in extremely complicated cases, such as patients with metal artefacts or root canal therapy. The method has been evaluated mainly from an algorithmic perspective, and the authors call for rigorous multicentre clinical trials.
